## How a Constrained Forward Model Solves the Next Instant {#sec-lay-ch18}

## A Concrete Picture

Imagine a computer model of two hinged arms holding a bar. You specify its
configuration, motion and applied joint torques. The program must find how the
arms and bar accelerate together. It cannot move each arm independently and
then declare that both hands still hold the same bar. Their shared geometry
helps determine the interaction forces.

A forward swing model performs this calculation repeatedly. Within a declared
contact mode, it balances inertia, gravity, velocity effects, applied loads and
constraint reactions. Flexible deformation and actuator memory add state variables that
must also evolve. If a hand slips or a contact opens, the equations governing
that mode must change; keeping every contact closed is not a universal success
criterion.

![A Schematic Forward-Dynamics Loop Connects State, Constrained Acceleration, Integration and Separate Numerical Audits.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_forward_solver_loop.svg){#fig-lay-forward-loop width=98% fig-alt="A schematic loop starts with complete state and inputs, solves a declared constraint mode, integrates to a candidate next state and checks numerical consistency; refinement compares separate runs."}

## How the Mechanism Works

For local generalized coordinates $\mathbf q$ with $\mathbf v=\dot{\mathbf q}$, write

$$
\mathbf M\dot{\mathbf v}+\mathbf h
=\mathbf Q+\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\lambda,
\qquad
\mathbf J\dot{\mathbf v}=\mathbf b.
$$

The vector $\boldsymbol\lambda$ contains reaction multipliers. The mass matrix
$\mathbf M$ expresses inertia and coupling. The constraint
Jacobian $\mathbf J$ maps coordinate velocities to rates of change of the
constraint equations. Here $\mathbf h$
contains the selected velocity, gravitational, elastic and dissipative terms;
$\mathbf Q$ contains the remaining applied loads. The allocation can differ
between implementations, but each term belongs in the balance once. An elastic
force already represented by a potential must not be added again as an
independent energy source. Representations with generalized velocities other
than $\dot{\mathbf q}$ require their own configuration-rate map.

For a fixed set of ideal bilateral constraints, the simultaneous solve has the
Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) saddle-point form

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf M&-\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\\
\mathbf J&\mathbf 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\dot{\mathbf v}\\\boldsymbol\lambda\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf Q-\mathbf h\\\mathbf b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The right-hand side $\mathbf b$ follows from differentiating the constraints,
including any prescribed boundary motion. Symmetric positive-definite $\mathbf M$ and
full row rank of $\mathbf J$ are sufficient for a unique solve in this form.
Redundant constraints, singular configurations and different contact laws need
separate treatment. Reaction multipliers are solved alongside acceleration;
they are not arbitrary controls chosen to create a preferred swing.

### What a Reaction Multiplier Means

The physical generalized reaction is $\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\lambda$.
A multiplier's units and sign depend on the constraint equation. Multiplying
one constraint row and its right-hand side by seven divides its multiplier by
seven while leaving the reaction and acceleration unchanged. A raw multiplier
is therefore not automatically a Cartesian hand-force component.

The same caution applies to residual norms. Translational and rotational force
equations, acceleration constraints and geometric closure have different units
and scales. Report them separately or normalize them with declared reference
scales. A small unscaled norm alone does not tell the reader which physical
quantity is accurate.

### Integration Turns Local Rules Into a Trajectory

An integrator approximates the coupled evolution of configuration, velocity and
internal states. It may evaluate dynamics several times per accepted step.
Large steps can miss events or distort fast flexible motion even when the
animation looks smooth. Stability, accuracy and constraint consistency are
related but distinct requirements.

Compare declared observables over a sequence of step sizes, solver tolerances
and, where relevant, mode-transition settings. Look for convergence and report
the range over which it is observed. Projection tolerances, event-location
error, roundoff and competing errors can prevent each residual from decreasing
monotonically. The name of an integration scheme does not establish its order
after velocity-dependent forces, projections or contact switches are added.

Define each event explicitly. In the revision-bound two-degree-of-freedom
double-pendulum study, “impact” is a
specified club-angle crossing located by interpolation; it does not simulate
ball contact. The planar forward two-hand example instead runs to a fixed
time horizon. Neither should be described as a resolved club-ball collision.
An actual collision requires an impact law or a resolved compliant-contact
model, with its own verification.

### Initial Conditions and Projection

For a holonomic constraint $\boldsymbol\Phi(\mathbf q,t)=\mathbf 0$,
compatible velocities satisfy the following condition, where
$\boldsymbol\Phi_t$ is the explicit partial derivative with respect to time:

$$
\mathbf J\mathbf v=-\boldsymbol\Phi_t.
$$

For a stationary boundary, $\boldsymbol\Phi_t=\mathbf 0$ and the condition
reduces to $\mathbf J\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$: admissible motion does not open or
stretch the constraints. Give
flexible modes, activation states and controller memory consistent initial
values too. Otherwise the solver may spend its first steps repairing the
initialization rather than predicting the intended experiment.

Projection changes a state to satisfy the chosen constraints. Its correction
and energy change are numerical bookkeeping, unless a separately justified
physical reset law gives them a different interpretation. Record whether the
energy ledger starts before or after initial projection. A genuine impact can
change velocity discontinuously; silently correcting an inconsistent measured
state is a different operation.

For a manufactured example at fixed configuration, take two translational
coordinates with masses $2$ and $1\,\mathrm{kg}$, velocity
$(3,-1)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and the stationary condition $v_1+v_2=0$.
Mass-metric velocity projection gives $(7/3,-7/3)\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Kinetic
energy changes from $9.5$ to $49/6\,\mathrm J$: a loss of
$4/3\,\mathrm J$ introduced by the correction. Calling that loss muscle work
or physical damping would tell the wrong story. Large corrections should
trigger investigation of initialization, discretization or model consistency.

### Inputs Need a Declared Physical Meaning

A finite step in directly applied torque produces a finite acceleration jump
in a regular fixed-mode model; it is not an impulse and does not itself jump
velocity. For example, a $3\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ step on an ideal rotor with
inertia $2\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ changes acceleration to
$1.5\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}$. Starting at $0.4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, speed is still
$0.4$ at the step and reaches $0.55\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ after $0.1\,\mathrm s$.
The increase in kinetic energy equals the torque's work in this example.

Realistic input models may add activation or transmission dynamics. A
first-order filter smooths its output but does not impose a universal hard
torque-rate bound. A delay shifts a signal without necessarily smoothing it.
Preload and actuator memory can retain applied load after the command is set
to zero. Rise-time and delay studies therefore compare different input models
and initializations; they do not directly identify human activation.

The pinned two-hand example maps its six command values directly to joint
torques. Its zero-command branch removes those torques. That interpretation
must be revised if an actuator state is inserted between command and load.

### Building a Counterfactual Correctly

At a forward intervention, copy the complete model state and preserve the
boundary prescription. Change only the declared future input, contact law or
other intervention variable. Keep solver settings comparable and record
mode changes. Do not silently reset velocities, controller integrators or shaft
modes. The trajectories can then diverge through both state evolution and
changed reactions.

For an instantaneous input comparison, retain the state and solve the dynamics
and reactions again under each input. If the applied generalized load has the
affine form $\mathbf Q=\mathbf Q_0+\mathbf B\mathbf u$, then $\mathbf Q_0$ is
the input-independent load and $\mathbf B$ maps inputs to generalized loads.
With all coefficients fixed at that state, the same nonsingular KKT system maps input differences
linearly to acceleration differences. Here $\mathbf u$ must be the declared
input level; it is not automatically the actuator command. Contact-mode changes
or nonlinear actuator maps can invalidate
that simple comparison. A zero-velocity construction changes the state and
requires a separate feasibility check; it is not another input change at the
original state. See @sec-lay-ch11 for the different counterfactual questions.

### Physical Work and Numerical Error Need Separate Ledgers

Choose the modeled system and its mechanical energy before assigning power.
Count applied work, prescribed-boundary power and dissipation consistently with
the conservative terms already included in that energy. An ideal stationary
constraint has zero net power across the complete constrained system, but a
hand force can still transfer energy into the club viewed alone.

An ideal moving constraint may supply or remove energy. In a second
manufactured example, two masses of $2$ and $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ satisfy
$q_1-q_2=s(t)$, where $q_1,q_2$ are their positions and $s(t)$ is a prescribed
relative displacement. With $\dot s=0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$,
$\ddot s=0.2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, velocities $(2,1.5)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and no
other loads, the reaction is $(0.24,-0.24)\,\mathrm N$. Its net power is
$0.12\,\mathrm W$, equal to the kinetic-energy rate. Resetting both velocities
to zero would violate the retained moving-boundary condition. Compliant contact
can store energy and may dissipate it; neither effect should be confused with
an ideal stationary reaction.

Record numerical projection energy separately from the physical work ledger.
A small net energy residual can conceal cancellation among larger numerical
errors. Momentum checks add useful information when the external wrench and
the reference point/frame are specified; angular momentum about a moving point
requires the appropriate transport terms.

### What the Pinned Forward Example Actually Shows

The saved planar two-hand example has seven coordinates, four independent
bilateral constraints and no prescribed swing trajectory. Its report records
closure, interface-power identities, work-energy residuals, geometry controls
and selected step/tolerance comparisons. These records support bounded
mechanical feasibility under the stated model, not a guarantee for every
forward tier or controller.

The saved baseline reports about $0.096\,\mathrm J$ of absolute work-energy
residual alongside about $-0.778\,\mathrm J$ of accumulated projection-energy
change. The latter is not physical work to insert merely to improve the former.
It shows why the separate error terms matter. In the saved step comparison,
the raw work-energy residual falls from about $0.695$ to $0.373$ to
$0.191\,\mathrm J$ as the step falls from $2$ to $1$ to $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$;
position closure does not decrease strictly at every refinement. These are
inspected stored results, not a new simulation performed for this chapter.

The model's direct tests also examine a short driven rollout, a zero-torque
step comparison, a branch from an achieved moving state, coincident grip offsets and selected
invalid requests. Their finite cases do not prove general convergence,
symplecticity or global positive definiteness. Checking a release's file hashes
establishes correspondence to recorded artifacts; rerunning its dynamics is a
separate act that must be reported separately.

### Inverse and Forward Models Complement Each Other

Inverse dynamics uses motion, inertial assumptions and external-load information
to infer net generalized loads. It does not uniquely recover individual muscle
forces or redundant internal contact forces without additional assumptions.
Forward dynamics predicts motion from a complete initial state and a declared
input model. It enables interventions within that model, but its parameter,
controller and contact assumptions remain consequential.

Agreement between inverse and forward calculations can expose implementation
errors. It can also follow from using the same equations and fitted data in both
directions. Independent observations and held-out interventions provide stronger
evidence for predictive validity than replay agreement alone.

**Model Result:** The revision-bound planar study reports selected numerical
checks and a feasible negative sum of grip-force moments about the club center,
using its declared planar angular sign convention and excluding direct wrist torques.
Those checks neither establish biological passivity nor identify a human
control strategy.

**Human Evidence:** MacKenzie and Sprigings fitted a selected swing of one
golfer using single-camera measurements; their quantitative comparison did not
cover the model's axial arm rotation. A separate optimization then targeted
clubhead speed [@mackenzie2009]. Balzerson and colleagues combined a fitted
golfer model with shaft, impact and flight components having different
comparison datasets [@balzerson2016]. These studies illustrate useful modeling
and bounded empirical comparisons, rather than independent validation of every
prediction of an optimized whole-system model.

**Hypothesis:** Mechanisms that survive declared forward, geometry and numerical
checks are stronger candidates for targeted experiments. That survival does
not establish that golfers exploit them.

**Practical Interpretation:** Trust grows when the reader can distinguish the
equations, their numerical solution, the fitted data and genuinely predictive
tests of the physical system.

### Coordinates, Contact and Independent Implementations

Minimal coordinates can eliminate simple holonomic joint constraints locally.
Maximal coordinates often make body poses and complex connectivity easier to
describe, at the cost of explicit constraints. Spatial-vector algorithms
organize dynamics calculations and can be used with different coordinate
choices; they are not a competing coordinate representation.

Compare mapped positions, velocities, wrenches and powers for the same physical
model, inputs and initial state. Components in different bases or at different
wrench reference points need the corresponding transformations. Coordinate
invariance is not a claim that kinetic energy has the same numerical value for
observers moving relative to one another. Agreement between independent engines
is strongest when they do not share the same derivative implementation or
unexamined assumptions.

An ideal bilateral grasp places no friction or strength limit on its reaction.
Human hands and feet do. A no-slip model must be checked against the specified
contact capacity before interpreting its loads physically. Unilateral contact
requires separation and admissibility conditions; an active-set KKT solve can
describe a regular fixed mode, while switching, complementarity, compliant
contact or impacts require additional equations and numerical choices. Test
sensitivity to those choices when the proposed mechanism depends on contact.

### Reader Lab: Separate a Broken Calculation From a Different Model

Introduce a frame mismatch deliberately: reverse one measured axis while
leaving the model transformation unchanged. A frame-consistency check should
detect that error. Transforming all quantities consistently describes the same
physics and should pass. Likewise, a documented damping removal or input delay
can define a legitimate new physical scenario. It should change predictions,
not automatically fail the solver. Energy may rise when applied work is positive.

For a geometry control, setting both grip offsets to zero removes their
force-generated moment about the coincident point. By contrast, reversing an
offset and solving a new trajectory also changes the reactions; the resultant
couple is not guaranteed to reverse sign. State the exact limiting prediction
before using it as a pass/fail test.

Next perturb the initial state or enlarge the timestep and compare correction
sizes and converged observables. Preserve failed cases and classify them:
infeasible contact, singular geometry, a numerical failure and a different
physical model are not interchangeable explanations. Do not loosen tolerances
until a desired animation appears and then call it verified.

### Reproducibility and Extending the Model

Record the exact code and model revision, parameters, complete initial state,
input schedule or feedback law, solver settings, event definitions and relevant
random seed. State units and frames in machine-readable outputs. A stateful
controller needs its own state evolution; repeatedly calling a hidden mutable
callback can change the experiment and make reconstructed diagnostics disagree
with the inputs actually used.

Retain earlier benchmarks when adding a shaft, moving base or spatial joint.
Add new limiting cases and explain which earlier assumptions no longer apply.
Version changed output meanings and regenerate figures from recorded results.
Publish a small runnable benchmark, its expected tolerances and failed-case
examples so review does not require the entire optimization stack.

The same reproducibility requirement extends to the reader's visualization.
An educational interface should consume the same versioned model or verified
outputs used for the scientific evidence. That is a design recommendation,
not proof that every existing front end already shares one engine. Inspect
actual dependencies before making that architectural claim.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The two-arm picture assumes known geometry, constitutive laws and boundaries.
Human anatomy, contact and control are uncertain. Verification checks how well
the implementation solves the declared equations; validation compares relevant
predictions with physical observations over a specified use range. Good
numerics can integrate an inadequate model, and a good fit can hide compensating
errors. Neither an optimized swing nor a small residual proves that a person
used the modeled controls, that a particular muscle supplied a net torque, or
that a proposed intervention is beneficial.
